findings.title: Boundary changed so orders of exactly 500 lose the extra discount
findings.explanation: The condition was changed from subtotal >= 500m to subtotal > 500m. The comment on line 24 still says orders of 500 or more get an extra 5 percent, so an order subtotal of exactly 500 now gets no extra discount. The code no longer matches its documented behaviour, and customers at that boundary are charged more.
findings.reason: Same defect: the strict > 500m check contradicts the '500 or more' comment, so exactly 500 misses the extra discount.

findings.title: Average price divides by line count instead of total quantity
findings.explanation: The previous code divided the subtotal by the sum of quantities, which gives the average price per item. The new code divides by items.Count, the number of order lines. For an order with one line of 3 units at 10m each, the subtotal is 30 and the result is 30 instead of 10. The method name and the old behaviour both indicate a per-unit average, so the result is wrong for any order with quantities above 1.
findings.reason: Covers the part of label 2 about dividing by line count instead of total quantity.

findings.title: Empty order throws DivideByZeroException
findings.explanation: The zero-count guard was removed. When lines is empty, Subtotal returns 0m and items.Count is 0. Dividing a decimal by zero throws DivideByZeroException, so an empty order crashes instead of returning a price.
findings.reason: Covers the part of label 2 about an empty order causing DivideByZeroException at line 45.

findings.title: SQL injection via unvalidated sortBy after allowlist check removed
findings.explanation: The change removed the SortColumns allowlist check that threw ArgumentException for unknown sort columns. The caller-supplied sortBy is now interpolated directly into the SQL text at the ORDER BY clause (line 28). An attacker-controlled value such as 'Amount; DROP TABLE dbo.Invoices--' or a subquery becomes executable SQL. Column names cannot be bound as parameters, so the allowlist was the only protection.
findings.reason: Reports the same SQL injection from unvalidated sortBy interpolated into ORDER BY, with the unused SortColumns allowlist.

findings.title: SqlConnection no longer disposed
findings.explanation: The connection was changed from 'await using var' to a plain 'var'. Nothing now disposes or closes it. The connection stays checked out of the ADO.NET connection pool until it is garbage collected, so repeated calls to DeleteOlderThanAsync exhaust the pool and cause timeouts, and the connection is also left open if OpenAsync or ExecuteNonQueryAsync throws.
findings.reason: Reports the same undisposed SqlConnection in DeleteOlderThanAsync leading to connection pool exhaustion.

findings.title: Password reset token generated with non-cryptographic System.Random
findings.explanation: The token is now produced by new Random().Next(100000, 999999).ToString(). System.Random is a predictable PRNG, and a fresh instance seeded from the clock can be reproduced by an attacker who knows roughly when the token was issued. The token is also only about 900,000 possible values, so it can be guessed by brute force without any rate limit in this code. This replaces the earlier 32-byte RandomNumberGenerator token, which was unguessable. The upper bound 999999 is also exclusive, so that value can never be issued.
findings.reason: Identifies the use of System.Random with a six-digit token on line 21, the same defect as label 1. The claim about an earlier 32-byte token is extra context, not a separate defect.

findings.title: Expiry comparison is inverted, accepting expired tokens and rejecting valid ones
findings.explanation: The condition saved.ExpiresAt > clock.GetUtcNow() returns false for tokens that are still valid and proceeds with tokens that have already expired. Every legitimate redemption within the 30-minute window fails, and any stale token that is still stored can be redeemed indefinitely. This is both a functional failure on normal input and a security hole in the expiry control.
findings.reason: Correctly identifies the inverted expiry comparison on line 29, which refuses valid tokens and accepts expired ones.

findings.title: Client-supplied file name used as storage path enables path traversal on upload
findings.explanation: storedName is now file.FileName, which is untrusted and not sanitized. A name such as "../../Program.cs" or an absolute path passes the extension check (Path.GetExtension still yields an allowed value), and Path.Combine(folder, storedName) then resolves outside the uploads folder. The file is written to an arbitrary location under the content root, which can overwrite application files or plant executable content.
findings.reason: Client-supplied file name used as the stored path allows traversal out of the uploads folder, which is the same defect as label 1.

findings.title: Fixed, user-chosen file name overwrites existing uploads
findings.explanation: With storedName equal to the original file name, WriteAllBytesAsync silently replaces any existing file with the same name. Two users uploading 'report.pdf' or a repeated upload of the same name destroys the earlier document, and the returned id no longer identifies a unique stored object. The previous GUID naming avoided this.
findings.reason: Describes cs-04-document-upload#1 but at lines 34-34, outside the window. Same-name uploads overwriting each other is the second half of label 1, which names the client-chosen file name on line 29.

findings.title: Removed traversal check lets Download read arbitrary files
findings.explanation: The guard rejecting ids containing '/', '\\' or '..' was deleted. The id is passed straight to Path.Combine, so an id such as "..%2F..%2Fappsettings.json" (after URL decoding) or a rooted path like "/etc/passwd" escapes the uploads folder. File.Exists then passes and PhysicalFile returns the file contents to the caller.
findings.reason: Download combines an unchecked id into a path, enabling arbitrary file read. This is the same as label 3.

findings.title: Synchronous copy buffers the whole file in memory and blocks the request thread
findings.explanation: The change replaces the streaming async CopyToAsync(target, ct) with a synchronous CopyTo into a MemoryStream, then calls ToArray, which makes a second full copy. Each request holds the file twice in memory and blocks a thread on I/O. The cancellation token is no longer honored during the copy.
findings.reason: Synchronous CopyTo into a MemoryStream followed by ToArray blocks a thread and buffers the whole file, which is label 2.

findings.title: Shared static non-thread-safe Dictionary used for cache
findings.explanation: The field was changed from an instance ConcurrentDictionary to a static Dictionary. Dictionary is not thread-safe, and GetRateAsync reads it (line 27) and writes it (line 36) from concurrent requests. Concurrent writes or a read during a resize can corrupt the dictionary, return wrong rates, or throw, and in older runtimes can cause an infinite loop. Making it static also shares the cache across all instances and DI scopes, so it is no longer scoped to the instance the constructor configured.
findings.reason: Identifies the static non-thread-safe Dictionary accessed concurrently at lines 27 and 36, the same defect as label #1.

findings.title: Blocking on async HTTP call with .Result
findings.explanation: ConvertAsync is async, but .Result synchronously blocks the calling thread until the HTTP request completes. Under load this ties up thread pool threads for the full network round trip, causing thread starvation. In contexts with a SynchronizationContext it can also deadlock. The await was removed for no reason.
findings.reason: Identifies blocking on .Result inside an async method, with thread starvation and deadlock risk, the same defect as label #2.

findings.title: Retry loop now makes only two attempts and fails with a misleading exception
findings.explanation: The loop bound changed from attempt <= MaxAttempts to attempt < MaxAttempts, so the loop runs only attempts 1 and 2. On attempt 2, a 429 or 5xx response still satisfies retryable && attempt < MaxAttempts (2 < 3), so the code sleeps and continues. The loop then exits and throws InvalidOperationException("Unreachable") even though the path is reachable. A persistent 5xx on the second attempt therefore produces a generic exception instead of the HTTP error, and the final attempt is never made. The catch filter has the same off-by-one problem: an HttpRequestException on attempt 2 is not caught, so it escapes without a retry.
findings.reason: Identifies the off-by-one loop bound at line 13 that allows only two attempts and ends in the misleading 'Unreachable' exception, which is the same defect as label #1.

findings.title: Per-call HttpClient bypasses the configured 'shipping' client and risks socket exhaustion
findings.explanation: The change replaces factory.CreateClient("shipping") with a new HttpClient on each call, disposed at the end. This discards whatever the named client configuration provides, such as default headers, authentication handlers, timeouts, and base address. Requests may then fail authentication or use the wrong endpoint. Creating a new HttpClient per call also defeats the handler pooling that IHttpClientFactory provides and can exhaust sockets under load. The base address is hardcoded, which duplicates configuration that belongs in the factory registration.
findings.reason: Identifies the per-call new HttpClient at line 40 that bypasses the configured 'shipping' factory client and risks socket exhaustion, matching label #2.

findings.title: End bound drops orders placed on the last day
findings.explanation: The doc comment says both the first and last day are included, but the change removed AddDays(1) from the end bound. The filter `o.PlacedAt < end` now uses midnight at the start of `to`, so every order placed on the `to` date is excluded from the report. This gives wrong totals on normal input.
findings.reason: Same defect: the end bound is midnight at the start of the last day with an exclusive filter, so the last day is excluded.

findings.title: All matching orders are loaded into memory and aggregated on the client
findings.explanation: The GroupBy, Count, Sum and OrderByDescending were removed from the database query. Now every order in the date range is materialized with ToListAsync and grouped in memory, so memory and transfer grow with the number of orders rather than the number of customers.
findings.reason: Loading all orders into memory and aggregating on the client is a genuine inefficiency. The label mentions it only as context for the N+1 issue, so it is not covered by a label of its own, but it is a valid performance defect.

findings.title: One database query per customer inside a loop
findings.explanation: For each customer group, `db.Customers.SingleAsync` issues a separate round trip to the database. A report covering N customers runs N+1 queries, and the cost grows linearly with the number of customers in the range.
findings.reason: Same N+1 defect: one Customers query per group inside the loop.

findings.title: Average throws on a customer with no orders
findings.explanation: The zero-count guard was removed. Enumerable.Average on an empty sequence of decimals throws InvalidOperationException. Any customer without orders now causes an unhandled exception instead of returning 0m.
findings.reason: Same defect: Average throws InvalidOperationException on an empty sequence for a customer with no orders.

findings.title: Hardcoded fallback JWT signing key
findings.explanation: When Jwt:SigningKey is missing, the code now falls back to the literal string "portal-dev-signing-key-change-me-0123456789", which is in source control. Anyone who knows this default can mint tokens that pass signature validation, so the portal can be accessed without valid credentials in any environment where the setting is absent. The previous code failed fast with an exception.
findings.reason: Identifies the hardcoded fallback signing key on line 11, the same defect as the label.

findings.title: Token lifetime validation disabled
findings.explanation: ValidateLifetime is set to false, so expired JWTs are accepted indefinitely as long as the signature is valid. Stolen or long-lived tokens never expire, and the ClockSkew setting has no effect.
findings.reason: Identifies ValidateLifetime = false, so expired tokens are accepted, the same defect as the label.

findings.title: Bearer token written to logs
findings.explanation: The warning log now includes the full Authorization header, which contains the bearer token. Anyone with access to the logs can take over the session of each rejected token, and tokens that are only partly valid are also exposed.
findings.reason: Identifies the Authorization header being written to the log on lines 34-35, the same defect as the label.

findings.title: Normalize throws on malformed UTF-16 input
findings.explanation: String.Normalize throws ArgumentException when the string contains invalid code points such as unpaired surrogates. ToSlug only guards against null, so a user-supplied title containing a lone surrogate makes the method throw instead of returning a slug.
findings.reason: The claim is accurate: string.Normalize throws ArgumentException on invalid UTF-16 such as a lone surrogate. ToSlug only guards against null, so a user-supplied title can make it throw instead of returning a slug. This is a minor edge case, but it is genuine and unlabeled.

findings.title: Subject claim lookup for "sub" can fail under default JWT bearer mapping
findings.explanation: CustomerId() calls User.FindFirst("sub"). With the default JwtBearer configuration (MapInboundClaims enabled), the JWT handler maps the inbound "sub" claim to ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier, so no "sub" claim is present on the principal. The method then throws InvalidOperationException for every authenticated request to Place and Get, which surfaces as a 500 on normal input.
findings.reason: Whether "sub" is remapped depends on authentication configuration that is not in this file. Apps commonly set MapInboundClaims=false or use another handler, and the code deliberately looks up "sub" and throws a clear error if it is missing. Nothing in the file shows the failure, so this is speculation, not a defect.

findings.title: Hardcoded credentials and keys in source
findings.explanation: The database password (admin123), an API key and an encryption key are compiled as constants. Anyone with access to the source or binary can read them, and rotating them requires a code change and redeploy.
findings.reason: Reports the hardcoded DB password and API key (lines 10-11) together; the encryption key at line 12 is a related constant.

findings.title: SQL injection via table name and user id
findings.explanation: tableName and userId are interpolated directly into the SQL text. A caller can pass userId like x' OR '1'='1 or a tableName that reads or alters other tables.
findings.reason: SQL injection through interpolated tableName and userId at line 26.

findings.title: OS command injection via cmd.exe
findings.explanation: The untrusted command string is appended to cmd.exe /c arguments. Shell metacharacters such as & or | let a caller run arbitrary commands on the server.
findings.reason: Command injection through cmd.exe /c with the caller's command.

findings.title: Path traversal in file read
findings.explanation: fileName is concatenated into a path under C:\UserFiles without validation. A value such as ..\..\Windows\win.ini escapes the directory and reads arbitrary files.
findings.reason: Path traversal via fileName concatenated into the file path.

findings.title: Cross-site scripting through unencoded comment
findings.explanation: The raw comment is embedded in HTML and returned to the client. A comment containing script markup executes in other users' browsers.
findings.reason: XSS from the unencoded comment embedded in HTML.

findings.title: Connection string with password placed in exception message
findings.explanation: The exception text includes the full connection string containing the database password and the username. It can be written to logs or returned to callers.
findings.reason: Connection string in the authentication-failed exception message.

findings.title: Connection string leaked in wrapped exception
findings.explanation: The SqlException is rethrown as a generic Exception that embeds ConnectionString, exposing the password to any caller or log that receives it.
findings.reason: Wrapped SqlException exposes the connection string.

findings.title: Weak DES encryption with hardcoded key and IV
findings.explanation: DES has a 56-bit key and is considered broken. The key and IV are the fixed literal "12345678", so identical inputs always produce identical ciphertext and anyone can decrypt the data.
findings.reason: Covers both the DES algorithm and the hardcoded key and IV.

findings.title: Predictable token from seeded System.Random
findings.explanation: System.Random with the fixed seed 123 produces the same sequence every time, so the generated security token is predictable and can be guessed.
findings.reason: Fixed-seed Random used for the security token.

findings.title: API key returned to caller on authentication
findings.explanation: The authentication result includes the static ApiKey constant, so every authenticated user receives the same shared key regardless of their identity or permissions.
findings.reason: API key returned to the caller on successful login.

findings.title: Plaintext password comparison in database
findings.explanation: The query compares the Password column directly with the supplied password, which implies passwords are stored in plaintext. A database leak then exposes every account password.
findings.reason: Plaintext password comparison in the query.

findings.title: Unsanitized user input written to log file
findings.explanation: The raw comment is appended to the log, so embedded newlines can forge log entries. The write is also synchronous inside a request handler.
findings.reason: Log injection is genuine: the raw comment is written to the log without sanitizing, and the entry has no newline separator. No label covers it.

findings.title: Unsynchronized static counter and blocking sleep
findings.explanation: _counter++ on a static field is not atomic, so concurrent callers can get duplicate ids. Thread.Sleep(1) also blocks the calling thread on every call.
findings.reason: Non-atomic static counter increment; the Thread.Sleep remark is extra.

findings.title: Shared SqlConnection opened in constructor
findings.explanation: One connection is opened per service instance and reused for every call. Concurrent async commands on one SqlConnection fail, and the connection is never disposed, leaking resources.
findings.reason: Connection opened in the constructor and never disposed.

findings.title: Resources created and not disposed inside loop
findings.explanation: Each of the million iterations creates a MemoryStream, a FileStream that creates a file, and an HttpClient. None are disposed, so file handles and sockets leak and the loop creates a million files.
findings.reason: Undisposed MemoryStream, FileStream and HttpClient created in the loop.

findings.title: User id written to console on every row
findings.explanation: Each row logs the user identifier to console output, which can expose personal identifiers in logs and adds per-row I/O.
findings.reason: Logging the user id to the console is minor, and the user id is not especially sensitive. It is speculative rather than a real defect.

findings.title: Interval never cleared (memory leak)
findings.explanation: The setInterval is created in useEffect but the effect returns no cleanup function, so the interval keeps running after unmount and logs forever.
findings.reason: Same defect: setInterval in useEffect with no cleanup.

findings.title: XSS via dangerouslySetInnerHTML with user data
findings.explanation: User-controlled name is rendered as raw HTML, allowing script/HTML injection from API data or form input.
findings.reason: XSS through dangerouslySetInnerHTML at line 25.

findings.title: Hardcoded API key and admin password in client code
findings.explanation: The API key and X-Admin-Password are embedded in the frontend bundle where anyone can read them. The admin password is sent to a plain HTTP endpoint.
findings.reason: Covers the hardcoded API key, the hardcoded admin password, and mentions it is sent to a plain HTTP endpoint.

findings.title: Passwords and API key stored in localStorage
findings.explanation: User passwords and the API key are persisted to localStorage, where any injected script or other page code can read them.
findings.reason: Passwords and API key stored in localStorage; both labels covered.

findings.title: SQL query built by string interpolation of user input
findings.explanation: The query is constructed with raw search input and logged; it is unused for filtering, misleading and a classic injection pattern if ever sent to a backend.
findings.reason: The query string is only logged and never executed; no SQL injection exists, and the finding itself admits it is unused.

findings.title: Search destroys the user list
findings.explanation: searchUsers replaces the users state with the filtered result, so clearing the search or typing again filters an already-filtered list and the original data is lost.
findings.reason: Search overwrites the users state with filtered results, losing the original list.

findings.title: Infinite loop in processUserData
findings.explanation: processed is only incremented when user.name is truthy; otherwise the while loop never advances and hangs the browser.
findings.reason: Infinite loop when user has no name.

findings.title: Concurrent update corrupts user list
findings.explanation: Responses are mapped to indices of the users array, overwriting unrelated users with name 'Updated-N' regardless of userId, and responses are never checked for ok status.
findings.reason: Response index used as array position, so the wrong users are updated and failures are ignored.

findings.title: Generates ~1 billion characters of data on click
findings.explanation: Creating 1,000,000 objects each with a 1000-element joined string freezes the UI and consumes huge memory; it is also appended on each click without limit.
findings.reason: A million large objects built and put into state on click.

findings.title: eval of user-supplied code
findings.explanation: executeUserScript runs arbitrary strings via eval, and is called with the search input on Enter and with user names embedded in code, enabling arbitrary script execution.
findings.reason: eval of user-supplied script at line 116.

findings.title: Untyped settings merge with any and no real defaults
findings.explanation: mergeUserSettings uses any and an empty object with no defaults, so it just copies the input (including prototype-polluting keys) and is unused.
findings.reason: Mentions copying prototype-polluting keys from the input into a plain object; it is the same defect as the prototype pollution label, though framed as quality.

findings.title: Missing key prop in list
findings.explanation: The mapped user card div has no key, causing React reconciliation warnings and incorrect updates when the list changes.
findings.reason: Missing key on list items.

findings.title: Sensitive data rendered in the UI
findings.explanation: Passwords and credit card numbers are displayed in plain text for every user on the dashboard.
findings.reason: Passwords and card numbers rendered on screen.

findings.title: User name injected into executed script
findings.explanation: The user name is interpolated into a JavaScript string passed to eval, so a crafted name can execute arbitrary code.
findings.reason: The user name is interpolated into script text passed to eval at line 159, a distinct injection path from the eval at line 116 and the Enter handler.

findings.title: Enter key evaluates search input as code
findings.explanation: Pressing Enter in the search box passes the raw input value to eval, letting any typed or pasted code run.
findings.reason: Enter key passes the search input to eval.

findings.title: Form data added without validation or typing
findings.explanation: Object.fromEntries yields FormDataEntryValue values (possibly File) cast to any, so the User shape (id missing) is violated and the password and card are kept in state.
findings.reason: The form data is cast to any and added to state without an id and as FormDataEntryValue, a genuine type and validation defect that no label covers.

findings.title: Loading state not accessible
findings.explanation: The loading indicator is a plain div without role or aria-live, so screen reader users are not informed when data loads.
findings.reason: An accessibility nicety on the loading indicator; not a defect that matters here.

findings.title: Error state not surfaced in UI and uses alert
findings.explanation: Fetch errors are only shown via alert with the raw error string, and there is no error boundary around the list rendering user-provided content.
findings.reason: A speculative UX and error-boundary suggestion; it also cites the wrong lines.

findings.title: SQL injection through @SortColumn in ORDER BY
findings.explanation: The change removed the whitelist check on @SortColumn (N'Name', N'Price', N'CreatedAt') and replaced QUOTENAME(@SortColumn) with the raw @SortColumn. The value is concatenated straight into the dynamic SQL text, so a caller can pass a value such as N'Name; DROP TABLE dbo.Products; --' or a subquery that reads other tables. sp_executesql runs whatever text is built, and @sortColumn is not parameterized, so the injection succeeds for any caller that can execute the procedure.
findings.reason: Reports SQL injection via unsanitized @SortColumn concatenated into the ORDER BY on line 14, the same defect as the label. The claim about a removed whitelist is extra narrative but the core defect is identical.

findings.title: Balance is read without locking and then overwritten, allowing overdrafts and lost updates
findings.explanation: The change replaced the atomic conditional UPDATE (Balance = Balance - @Amount WHERE Balance >= @Amount) with a plain SELECT into @Balance and then an unconditional UPDATE that writes @Balance - @Amount. Under the default READ COMMITTED isolation level the SELECT takes no update lock and releases its shared lock immediately. Two concurrent transfers from the same account can both read a sufficient balance, both pass the check at line 17, and both write, so the account goes negative. A transfer that commits between the read and the write is also overwritten by the stale computed value, which loses money.
findings.reason: Describes the unlocked read followed by a write of the stale computed balance, which allows overdrafts and lost updates. This is the same defect as label #1.

findings.title: SET XACT_ABORT ON was removed, so errors can leave the transaction open or partly applied
findings.explanation: The change deletes SET XACT_ABORT ON. Without it, a run-time error that is not a deadlock or a severe error (for example a constraint violation on the Transfers insert or the balance update) only aborts the failing statement. Control then continues to the next statement with the transaction still open. The COMMIT at line 40 may never run, so the procedure can return to the caller with an open transaction holding locks, or with one leg of the transfer applied and the other not.
findings.reason: Describes the missing SET XACT_ABORT ON, which leaves the transaction open or partly applied when a statement fails. This is the same defect as label #2.

findings.title: NOT IN returns no rows if the subquery yields any NULL CustomerId
findings.explanation: The change replaces NOT EXISTS with NOT IN. If dbo.Orders.CustomerId is nullable and any order in the requested year has a NULL CustomerId, the NOT IN predicate evaluates to UNKNOWN for every customer, so the procedure returns an empty result set. NOT EXISTS does not have this problem, and the original version was correct for this case.
findings.reason: Reports the NOT IN with a NULL CustomerId in the subquery yielding UNKNOWN and returning no rows; same defect as label 1. References to a prior version are extra but the defect is the same.

findings.title: Wrapping OrderDate in YEAR() prevents a seekable range predicate
findings.explanation: The previous code used a half-open range (OrderDate >= @From AND OrderDate < @To), which lets SQL Server seek on an index on OrderDate. YEAR(o.OrderDate) = @Year applies a function to the column, so the optimizer must scan and evaluate every order row. The cost grows with the total order history, not just the rows for the year.
findings.reason: Reports YEAR() on OrderDate making the predicate non-sargable and preventing an index seek; same defect as label 2.

findings.title: Row-by-row cursor replaces a set-based UPDATE
findings.explanation: The change replaces one set-based UPDATE joining Products to staging.PriceChanges with a cursor that fetches each staging row and runs a separate UPDATE on dbs.Products per Sku. Each iteration is a separate statement and index seek, so runtime and log volume grow linearly with the batch size and with per-statement overhead. The same result is achievable in one statement, and the cursor adds no correctness benefit here.
findings.reason: Describes the row-by-row cursor UPDATE that should be one set-based join UPDATE, matching label 1.

findings.title: @@IDENTITY can return an identity value from a trigger instead of ImportLog
findings.explanation: @@IDENTITY returns the last identity value generated in the session by any scope, including triggers fired by the INSERT on line 25. SCOPE_IDENTITY() was correct because it is limited to the current scope. If dbo.ImportLog has an AFTER INSERT trigger that inserts into another identity table, @LogId gets that table's identity, and line 31 then stamps staging.PriceChanges with the wrong log id.
findings.reason: Identifies @@IDENTITY returning a trigger's identity instead of the ImportLog row's id, with SCOPE_IDENTITY() as the fix, matching label 2.

findings.title: OUTPUT parameter keeps a caller-supplied value when no customer matches
findings.explanation: @CustomerId is an OUTPUT parameter, so a caller can pass a non-NULL value in. The SELECT at lines 15-17 assigns nothing when no row matches Email, so the variable keeps that value. The IF @CustomerId IS NULL test at line 19 then fails, and the procedure runs the UPDATE at lines 28-30 against whatever CustomerId the caller passed. A new email can therefore silently overwrite another customer's name and never be inserted, and the procedure returns that id as if it were the match.
findings.reason: This is a genuine bug. In T-SQL an OUTPUT parameter is bidirectional, and `SELECT @var = col` leaves the variable unchanged when no row matches. A caller who passes a non-NULL @CustomerId, for example a reused variable in a loop, skips the insert and updates the wrong customer. The fix is to set @CustomerId = NULL before the SELECT.

findings.title: Unencoded user input in query string
findings.explanation: The search term is interpolated into the URL without encodeURIComponent. Characters such as &, #, + and = are interpreted by the server. A query like "abc&limit=10000" adds parameters, and "abc#x" truncates the query. The term can also change the path or parameters the server sees, so the request no longer means what the user typed.
findings.reason: Reports the missing encodeURIComponent on the search term in the fetch URL, which is the same defect as label 2.

findings.title: Effect cleanup removed; stale and in-flight requests overwrite newer state
findings.explanation: The cleanup that cleared the timer and aborted the controller was removed. When query changes or the component unmounts, the previous timer still fires and its fetch is not aborted. Responses can arrive out of order, so an older query's results or error can overwrite the results for the current query. Pending timers also keep running after unmount.
findings.reason: Describes ts-01-product-search#1 but at lines 36-37, outside the window. Reports the missing effect cleanup (timer not cleared, fetch not aborted), so stale responses can overwrite newer results. This is label 1; the cited lines are the end of the effect where the cleanup should be.

findings.title: taxCents no longer rounds to whole cents
findings.explanation: The change removes Math.round, so taxCents returns a fractional cent value such as 123.45 for a 1000-cent amount at 12.345%. Money in this module is otherwise integer cents (subtotalCents, applyCoupon, formatCents divides by 100). Callers that add this tax to a cents total or pass it to formatCents will produce fractional totals and inconsistent rounding.
findings.reason: Reports that taxCents returns unrounded fractional cents on line 26, which is the same defect as label 1.

findings.title: NaN and non-integer quantities now pass validation
findings.explanation: The Number.isInteger check was removed. For input such as "abc", Number(input) is NaN, and both NaN < 1 and NaN > 99 evaluate to false, so the function returns NaN as a quantity. For input such as "1.5" it returns 1.5, which passes the range test. Downstream quantity math then yields NaN or fractional line totals in subtotalCents.
findings.reason: Reports that NaN and fractional quantities pass the range check on line 31, because NaN fails both comparisons. This is the same defect as label 2.

findings.title: Password logged to the console
findings.explanation: The added console.debug call writes the user's plaintext password to the browser console on every sign-in attempt. Anyone with access to the console, error reporting that captures console output, or shared devices can read the credential.
findings.reason: Reports the plaintext password being written to the console via console.debug on line 19, the same defect as the label.

findings.title: Open redirect via unvalidated returnUrl
findings.explanation: The change removed the safeReturnUrl call and now assigns params.get("returnUrl") directly to window.location.assign. An attacker can craft a sign-in link with returnUrl=https://evil.example, and after a successful login the user is sent to an external site, which enables phishing. Only the fallback is safe; any absolute or protocol-relative URL is accepted. Note that the safeReturnUrl helper is now unused.
findings.reason: Reports the unvalidated returnUrl passed to window.location.assign on line 35 and the unused safeReturnUrl helper, the same open redirect as the label.

findings.title: Effect no longer re-runs when userId changes
findings.explanation: The dependency array was changed from [userId] to []. The effect fetches /api/profiles/${userId}, so when the userId prop changes the component keeps showing the previous user's profile, and a stale response can still be applied for the old user.
findings.reason: Identifies the empty dependency array on the effect that uses userId, so the profile is not reloaded when the user changes.

findings.title: Mutating state and calling setProfile with the same reference
findings.explanation: profile.tags.push(tag) mutates the existing state object in place, and setProfile(profile) passes the same reference back. React uses Object.is to detect changes, so it bails out of re-rendering for the profile update. The tag list only appears to update because setNewTag('') happens to trigger a render. Mutated state also breaks memoization and makes behavior dependent on unrelated state updates.
findings.reason: Identifies in-place mutation via push and setProfile with the same reference, which defeats React's change detection. The extra remark that setNewTag causes a re-render is accurate and does not change the match.

findings.title: SQL injection via string concatenation of route parameter
findings.explanation: The query now builds SQL by concatenating the raw req.params.id into the statement instead of passing it as a bind parameter. The parseInt check on line 9-10 only validates the parsed value, but the original unparsed string is what gets concatenated. An input such as "1 OR 1=1" passes validation (parseInt yields 1) and is sent to the database unchanged, so an attacker can read arbitrary rows or run other SQL.
findings.reason: Describes SQL injection from concatenating raw req.params.id, noting parseInt validation does not protect it; same as label 1.

findings.title: Ownership check removed, exposing other customers' orders
findings.explanation: The removed query filtered on customer_id = req.user.id, so only the requesting user's orders were returned. The replacement query filters only on id, so any authenticated user can fetch any order by id, including customer_id, total_cents and status for other customers. This is an insecure direct object reference.
findings.reason: Describes the missing customer_id ownership check on the order read, letting any user fetch any order; same as label 2.

findings.title: Internal error details and stack traces returned to clients
findings.explanation: The error handler now sends String(err) and the stack trace in the JSON body of every 500 response. This exposes internal file paths, library versions, and possibly SQL or connection details to any caller who triggers an error.
findings.reason: Describes the error handler returning String(err) and stack traces to clients; same as label 3.

findings.title: toDate shifts every date forward one month
findings.explanation: CalendarDay months are 1-12, but the change removed the `- 1` offset when calling the Date constructor, which expects 0-11. For example, { year: 2024, month: 1, day: 15 } now produces February 15, 2024. This also breaks addDays, which calls toDate, and isWeekend, which evaluates the weekday of the shifted date.
findings.reason: Identifies the missing month - 1 offset in toDate at line 9, which shifts every date one month forward and breaks addDays and isWeekend.

findings.title: fromDate returns the weekday instead of the day of the month
findings.explanation: date.getDay() returns the day of the week (0-6), not the day of the month. The day field should use getDate(). As written, fromDate returns a day value between 0 and 6, so addDays returns wrong dates, such as day 0 for dates that should be the 1st of a month.
findings.reason: Identifies that fromDate uses getDay() (weekday) instead of getDate() (day of month) at line 13.

findings.title: Delays above the timer limit fire repeatedly at 1 ms
findings.explanation: setInterval stores its delay as a signed 32-bit integer. For delayMs above 2147483647 (about 24.8 days), browsers and Node.js reset the delay to 1 ms, so the callback runs about 1000 times per second instead of rarely. The hook accepts any number and does not guard against this.
findings.reason: The 32-bit timer overflow is real platform behavior, but a delay above 24.8 days is not a realistic input for this hook. Guarding against it would be speculative hardening, and the code has no actual defect here.

findings.title: crypto.randomUUID may be unavailable
findings.explanation: crypto.randomUUID() is only exposed in secure contexts (HTTPS or localhost) and in fairly recent browsers. In an insecure context or an older environment, calling add() throws a TypeError inside the event handler, so the user cannot add any to-do.
findings.reason: crypto.randomUUID is widely supported in modern browsers and secure contexts. Flagging it is speculative environment-compatibility advice, not a defect in this code. The file has no known defects.
